query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: During cooling from a high-temperature BCC state, the Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy first undergoes spinodal decomposition within the disordered BCC phase, separating into a Ni–Al-lean BCC1 phase and a Ni–Al-rich BCC2 phase. As cooling continues below the ordering transition temperature, the Ni–Al-rich BCC2 phase orders into B2 particles, resulting in a hierarchical, reciprocal BCC/B2 microstructure that impedes dislocation motion and increases hardness.
generation.material_initial_state: Nominal Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 (at.%) high-entropy alloy, produced via vacuum-arc melting and casting, homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h under Ar, hot-forged, re-homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, and water-quenched.
generation.intervention: Specimens were annealed under Ar at 1100 °C for 1 h or at 1200 and 1300 °C for 30 min followed by water quenching, to induce different extents of spinodal decomposition and ordering during cooling.
generation.conditions: Annealing temperatures spanning 1100–1300 °C under argon with subsequent rapid water quenching. Characterization using Rockwell C hardness tests (1471 N load, 5 s dwell), XRD, SEM, SADP/dark-field TEM, and STEM–EDS mapping.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchical microstructure featuring a Ni–Al-lean BCC matrix interspersed with Ni–Al-rich ordered B2 nanoparticles, along with larger B2 particles that may contain embedded Ni–Al-lean BCC nanoparticles. Minor FCC phases (including grain-boundary Widmanstätten side-plates) may be present.
generation.mechanism: The high-temperature disordered BCC phase enters a miscibility gap during cooling, undergoing an initial spinodal decomposition into Ni–Al-lean (BCC1) and Ni–Al-rich (BCC2) regions. On further cooling below the ordering transition temperature, the Ni–Al-rich BCC2 regions order into the B2 phase. This sequential decomposition and ordering set up chemical partitioning that drives the formation of phase boundaries, refining microstructural features that obstruct dislocation motion and thereby raise the hardness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the 1100 °C annealed-and-quenched baseline (which has a near-equal BCC/FCC mix and lower hardness), specimens quenched from 1200 °C and especially from 1300 °C will show a larger fraction of BCC, a more pronounced spinodal decomposition signature with a higher density of ordered B2 precipitates, and ultimately exhibit higher hardness values.
generation.baseline: The baseline is defined by the 1100 °C annealed-and-water-quenched condition that resulted in a near-equal mix of BCC/FCC phases and the lowest measured hardness, representing the undecomposed high-temperature BCC state prior to significant spinodal decomposition and ordering.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid for Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloys subjected to annealing in the 1100–1300 °C temperature range under an inert atmosphere (Ar) with rapid water quenching. It may not apply if the alloy undergoes annealing conditions outside this range or if cooling rates are insufficient to ‘freeze in’ the microstructural features from sequential spinodal decomposition and ordering.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports a temperature-dependent evolution of hierarchical BCC/B2 microstructures and corresponding hardness increases, precise quantification of the sequential spinodal decomposition stages and their nanoparticle compositions remains uncertain due to current resolution limits in nanoscale chemical mapping.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 specimens and anneal them at 1100 °C, 1200 °C, and 1300 °C under argon for the specified durations before water quenching. Perform quantitative phase analysis using XRD and high-resolution TEM complemented by STEM–EDS to assess the presence, fraction, and chemical composition of the BCC, B2, and any FCC phases. Simultaneously, measure mechanical properties via Rockwell C hardness testing.
measurements: Rockwell C hardness for each annealing condition.
XRD analysis to quantify phase fractions (BCC, FCC, presence of B2 superlattice reflections).
TEM imaging (including dark-field techniques) to identify the microstructural morphology of the BCC and B2 phases.
STEM–EDS mapping/line scans to confirm chemical partitioning (Ni–Al enrichment in B2 particles versus Co–Cr–Fe enrichment in the BCC matrix).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens annealed at higher temperatures (1200 °C and 1300 °C) do not exhibit a progressively increasing BCC fraction, more pronounced and frequent B2 precipitates with the expected Ni–Al enrichment, and correspondingly higher hardness relative to the 1100 °C annealed baseline, then the proposed sequential spinodal decomposition and ordering mechanism is falsified.
